title: Look to others (Philippians 1:27–2:4)
hookLine: do nothing out of selfish ambition; look to others' interests

cards: Being Romans. That's how the crowd at Philippi puts it in the book of Acts, dragging Paul before the magistrates: these men teach customs that aren't lawful for us to keep, being Romans.

Acts calls the city a colony, a piece of Rome set down in Macedonia. So when Paul writes to the church in Philippi about how to live, he reaches for a word every one of them knew: the word for being a citizen.

teach.b: The King James Bible says: "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ." Conversation, in old English, meant your whole way of life, not just talk.

But Paul's Greek word is politeuesthe: live as citizens worthy of the good news. Later in the letter he'll say their real citizenship is in heaven. You know how to be Roman; now be citizens of something else, together.
Then he asks for something hard, and asks it warmly.
If there's any comfort in Christ, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tenderness, then "Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind."

teach.h: MAKE MY JOY COMPLETE: BE OF ONE MIND.
teach.b: Make my joy complete by getting along. It seems the Philippians had some friction; later he names two women who need to agree.
Then the heart of it: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves."

teach.h: NO EMPTY GLORY; HUMILITY AS A VIRTUE.
teach.b: Vainglory is empty glory: doing things to look good. Lowliness of mind is humility. Some readers point out that in ordinary Greek, lowly could mean servile, beneath you, and Paul turns it into something to aim for.

teach.h: YOUR OWN THINGS, AND ALSO OTHERS'.
teach.b: Then: "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others." Notice the small word also.

teach.h: LOOK NOT EVERY MAN ON HIS OWN THINGS.
teach.b: Paul doesn't say ignore your own needs. He says don't stop at them. It's a picture of a community where everyone quietly watches out for someone else, and someone else watches out for them.
Tomorrow, Paul gives the reason: the pattern of Christ himself.

how: Some Christian communities take Philippians 2:3–4 as a rule for their life together, and it is often read when churches, families or teams are working through conflict.

o: empty glory: doing things just to look good
a soldier's honor won bravely in battle
pride in your city's Roman citizenship

games.q: what's inside Philippians 1:27–2:4 — tap the pairs.
p: a Roman colony, proud of it
empty glory, doing it to look good
your own things, and others' too

s: 'conversation' in the KJV here means talking
it meant your whole way of life. Paul's Greek word means living as citizens.
Paul tells the Philippians to ignore their own needs
"look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others." also, not only.
doing things to look good. Paul says let nothing be done through it.

games.q: you're writing to a church that's proud of its Roman citizenship, and there's friction among them. what picture do you reach for?
o: tell them to stop being Roman.
tell them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel.
tell them to choose a leader to settle it.
games.why: Paul uses their own civic word, politeuesthe: live as citizens, worthy of the gospel, of one mind.

practice: Think of the people you'll be around today and pick one. What do they need that you could notice: the last good parking spot, the chance to finish their story, credit for their idea, the bigger slice?
Choose one way to put their interest ahead of yours without making a show of it, and if you pray, ask for eyes to see what others need.

wordCard.voice: Vainglory. Paul's word for empty glory, doing things to look good: he asks a proud Roman colony to let humility and others' needs come first instead.

orig.note: Greek: live as citizens. from polis, city. the KJV renders it 'let your conversation be'.

carryVoice: Your line: others first. Your own things, and also the things of others. See you tomorrow.
